imo-isl-2010-a2.title: Shift every variable by 1
imo-isl-2010-a2.body:
Expanding $(a-1)^4=a^4-4a^3+6a^2-4a+1$ and summing over the four variables,
$$\sum (a-1)^4=\sum a^4-4\sum a^3+6\sum a^2-4\sum a+4 .$$
Hence
$$4\sum a^3-\sum a^4=-\sum(a-1)^4+6\cdot 12-4\cdot 6+4=52-\sum (a-1)^4 .$$
Put $x=a-1,\ y=b-1,\ z=c-1,\ t=d-1$. Then
$$x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2=\sum a^2-2\sum a+4=12-12+4=4,$$
and the claim $36\le 52-(x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4)\le 48$ becomes
$$4\le x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4\le 16 .$$

**Lower bound.** By the power mean (or Cauchy–Schwarz) inequality,
$$x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4\ge \frac{(x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2)^2}{4}=\frac{16}{4}=4 .$$

**Upper bound.** Expanding,
$$(x^2+y^2+z^2+t^2)^2=(x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4)+2\sum_{\text{pairs}}x^2y^2\ \ge\ x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4,$$
so $x^4+y^4+z^4+t^4\le 4^2=16$.

Both bounds are sharp: the lower one at $(a,b,c,d)=(3,1,1,1)$, the upper one at $(0,2,2,2)$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-a3.title: Pair the terms and use AM–GM
imo-isl-2010-a3.body:
**Construction.** Let $x_{2i}=0$ and $x_{2i-1}=\tfrac12$ for $i=1,\dots,50$. Every three consecutive terms sum to at most $\tfrac12+0+\tfrac12=1$, and $S=50\cdot\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=\tfrac{25}{2}$.

**Bound.** Split $S$ into the $50$ pairs
$$x_{2i-1}x_{2i+1}+x_{2i}x_{2i+2}\qquad(i=1,\dots,50);$$
together (with the cyclic convention) they contain every term $x_jx_{j+2}$ exactly once. Fix $i$. The conditions for the triples starting at $2i-1$ and at $2i$ give
$$x_{2i-1}\le 1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1},\qquad x_{2i+2}\le 1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1}.$$
As all numbers are nonnegative,
$$x_{2i-1}x_{2i+1}+x_{2i}x_{2i+2}\le (1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1})x_{2i+1}+x_{2i}(1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1})=(x_{2i}+x_{2i+1})\bigl(1-x_{2i}-x_{2i+1}\bigr).$$
With $u=x_{2i}+x_{2i+1}$, AM–GM gives $u(1-u)\le\left(\frac{u+(1-u)}{2}\right)^2=\frac14$. Summing over $i=1,\dots,50$,
$$S\le 50\cdot\frac14=\frac{25}{2}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{25}{2}$**

imo-isl-2010-a3.title: Bound through the total sum
imo-isl-2010-a3.body:
Let $\Sigma=\sum x_i$. From $x_{i+2}\le 1-x_i-x_{i+1}$,
$$S\le\sum x_i(1-x_i-x_{i+1})=\Sigma-\sum x_i^2-\sum x_ix_{i+1}=\Sigma-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{100}(x_i+x_{i+1})^2 ,$$
because $\sum (x_i+x_{i+1})^2=2\sum x_i^2+2\sum x_ix_{i+1}$ (cyclically). By the QM–AM inequality, $\sum (x_i+x_{i+1})^2\ge\frac1{100}\left(\sum(x_i+x_{i+1})\right)^2=\frac{(2\Sigma)^2}{100}$. Hence
$$S\le \Sigma-\frac{2\Sigma^2}{100}=\frac{2}{100}\,\Sigma\left(50-\Sigma\right)\le\frac{2}{100}\cdot 25^2=\frac{25}{2},$$
by AM–GM on $\Sigma$ and $50-\Sigma$. The example $x_{\text{odd}}=\tfrac12$, $x_{\text{even}}=0$ attains it.

**Answer: $\dfrac{25}{2}$**

imo-isl-2010-a5.title: Injective, multiplicative, then a prime-exponent argument
imo-isl-2010-a5.body:
Call the equation $(1)$.

**Check.** For $f(x)=1/x$: $f(f(x)^2y)=\dfrac{1}{y/x^2}=\dfrac{x^2}{y}=x^3\cdot\dfrac{1}{xy}=x^3f(xy)$.

**Injectivity.** With $y=1$: $f(f(x)^2)=x^3f(x)$ $(2)$. If $f(x)=f(y)$, then $x^3=\dfrac{f(f(x)^2)}{f(x)}=\dfrac{f(f(y)^2)}{f(y)}=y^3$, so $x=y$.

**Multiplicativity.** By $(2)$ for $xy$, then $(1)$, then $(1)$ applied to the pair $(y,f(x)^2)$:
$$f\big(f(xy)^2\big)=(xy)^3f(xy)=y^3\cdot x^3f(xy)=y^3f\big(f(x)^2y\big)=f\big(f(y)^2f(x)^2\big).$$
By injectivity $f(xy)^2=f(x)^2f(y)^2$, and since values are positive, $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$. In particular $f(1)=f(1)^2$, so $f(1)=1$, and $f(x^n)=f(x)^n$ for all integers $n$.

**A relation for $f\circ f$.** Using multiplicativity on both sides of $(1)$: $f(f(x))^2f(y)=x^3f(x)f(y)$, so
$$f(f(x))=\sqrt{x^3f(x)} .\qquad(3)$$

**The function $g(x)=xf(x)$.** Using multiplicativity and $(3)$,
$$g(g(x))=xf(x)\cdot f\big(xf(x)\big)=xf(x)\cdot f(x)\,f(f(x))=xf(x)^2\sqrt{x^3f(x)}=\big(xf(x)\big)^{5/2}=g(x)^{5/2}.$$
Applying this to $g^{k-1}(x)$ repeatedly gives, for every $n\ge1$,
$$\underbrace{g(g(\cdots g}_{n+1}(x)\cdots))=g(x)^{(5/2)^n}.$$
The left side is a positive rational number. Suppose $g(x)\ne1$ and write $g(x)=p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_k^{\alpha_k}$ with distinct primes and nonzero integers $\alpha_i$. Then the right side has prime factorization $p_1^{(5/2)^n\alpha_1}\cdots p_k^{(5/2)^n\alpha_k}$, so $(5/2)^n\alpha_1=5^n\alpha_1/2^n$ must be an integer for every $n$ — false once $2^n\nmid\alpha_1$. Hence $g(x)=1$ for all $x$, i.e. $f(x)=\dfrac1x$.

**Answer:** $f(x)=\dfrac1x$ is the only solution. ∎

imo-isl-2010-a6.title: Find the minima, then the values above them
imo-isl-2010-a6.body:
Write $\mathbb N$ for the positive integers and $h^k$ for the $k$-fold iterate.

**Basic facts.** Iterating, $f(g^k(x))=f(x)+k$ and $g(f^k(x))=g(x)+k$. Let $a=\min f$, $b=\min g$, attained at $n_f$, $n_g$. Then $f(g^k(n_f))=a+k$, so **$f$ takes every integer value $\ge a$**; likewise $g$ takes every value $\ge b$.

If $f(x)=f(y)$ then $g(x)=g(f(x))-1=g(f(y))-1=g(y)$, and symmetrically. Write $x\sim y$ when $f(x)=f(y)$ (equivalently $g(x)=g(y)$).

**Claim 1.** Two different integers $\ge a$ are never similar (and likewise for integers $\ge b$).
*Proof.* Any $u,v\ge a$ are values of $f$: $u=f(x)$, $v=f(y)$. If $u\sim v$ then $g(f(x))=g(f(y))$, so $g(x)=g(y)$, so $x\sim y$ and $u=f(x)=f(y)=v$. The case $\ge b$ is symmetric. $\square$

**Claim 2.** $f(a)>a$ and $g(b)>b$. Otherwise $f(a)=a$ and then $g(a)=g(f(a))=g(a)+1$, absurd.

**Claim 3.** $a=b$.
*Proof.* By symmetry assume $a\le b$. Since $f(a)-1\ge a$, there is $x$ with $f(x)=f(a)-1$. Then $f(a)=f(x)+1=f(g(x))$, so $a\sim g(x)$. Both $a$ and $g(x)\ge b\ge a$ are integers $\ge a$, so by Claim 1, $a=g(x)\ge b$. Hence $a=b$. $\square$

**Claim 4.** $f(a)=g(a)=a+1$.
*Proof.* Suppose $f(a)\ge a+2$. Choose $x$ with $f(x)=f(a)-2\ \ (\ge a)$ and, since $g(x)\ge b=a$, choose $y$ with $f(y)=g(x)$. Then
$$f(a)=f(x)+2=f\big(g(g(x))\big),$$
so $a\sim g^2(x)$, and $g^2(x)\ge a$; by Claim 1, $a=g^2(x)=g(f(y))=g(y)+1\ge a+1$, a contradiction. So $f(a)=a+1$ (by Claim 2), and $g(a)=a+1$ in the same way. $\square$

**Claim 5.** $f(x)=g(x)=x+1$ for all $x\ge a$.
*Proof.* Induction on $x$, base $x=a$ by Claim 4. If $f(x)=g(x)=x+1$, then $f(x+1)=f(g(x))=f(x)+1=x+2$ and $g(x+1)=g(f(x))=g(x)+1=x+2$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** For any $n$, $g(n)\ge b=a$, so by Claim 5, $f(g(n))=g(n)+1$. But $f(g(n))=f(n)+1$. Hence $f(n)=g(n)$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-a8.title: Roots of an auxiliary cubic
imo-isl-2010-a8.body:
Let $\sigma=ac+ce+ae$ and $\tau=bd+bf+df$. Consider
$$P(x)=T(x-a)(x-c)(x-e)+S(x-b)(x-d)(x-f)=T(x^3-Sx^2+\sigma x-ace)+S(x^3-Tx^2+\tau x-bdf).$$
It is a cubic with leading coefficient $S+T>0$. Using $a<b<c<d<e<f$:
$$P(a)=S(a-b)(a-d)(a-f)<0,\quad P(c)=S(c-b)(c-d)(c-f)>0,$$
$$P(e)=S(e-b)(e-d)(e-f)<0,\quad P(f)=T(f-a)(f-c)(f-e)>0.$$
By the intermediate value theorem each of $(a,c)$, $(c,e)$, $(e,f)$ contains a root; a cubic has at most three roots, so its roots $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are real and **distinct**, and $P(x)=(S+T)(x-\alpha)(x-\beta)(x-\gamma)$. Comparing coefficients (Vieta),
$$\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\frac{2ST}{S+T},\qquad \alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha=\frac{S\tau+T\sigma}{S+T}.$$
Since the roots are distinct,
$$0<(\alpha-\beta)^2+(\beta-\gamma)^2+(\gamma-\alpha)^2=2(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-6(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha),$$
so
$$\frac{4S^2T^2}{(S+T)^2}>\frac{3(S\tau+T\sigma)}{S+T}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 4S^2T^2>3(S+T)(S\tau+T\sigma).$$
Both sides are positive, so taking square roots gives
$$2ST>\sqrt{3(S+T)\big(S(bd+bf+df)+T(ac+ae+ce)\big)}. \qquad ∎$$

imo-isl-2010-c1.title: Multiply small examples
imo-isl-2010-c1.body:
Call an order *good* if it satisfies all wishes, and say a number $N$ is *$k$-realizable* if some $k$ singers with suitable wishes have exactly $N$ good orders. The answer is **yes**.

**Lemma.** If $n_1$ is $k_1$-realizable and $n_2$ is $k_2$-realizable, then $n_1n_2$ is $(k_1+k_2)$-realizable.

*Proof.* Take singers $A_1,\dots,A_{k_1}$ realizing $n_1$ and $B_1,\dots,B_{k_2}$ realizing $n_2$, and add to every $B_j$ the wish to perform after all the $A_i$. A good order of the whole group is then exactly a good order of the $A$'s followed by a good order of the $B$'s, so there are $n_1n_2$ of them. $\square$

Since $2010=5\cdot 6\cdot 67$, it suffices to realize $5$ with $4$ singers, $6$ with $3$ singers and $67$ with $13$ singers ($4+3+13=20$).

- **5 with 4 singers** $a,b,c,d$: $c$ wants to come after $a$ and $b$; $d$ wants to come after $b$. The good orders are $abcd,\ abdc,\ bacd,\ badc,\ bdac$ — exactly $5$.
- **6 with 3 singers** with no wishes: $3!=6$ orders.
- **67 with 13 singers** $a_1,\dots,a_{11},x,y$: each $a_{i+1}$ wants to come after $a_i$ (so $a_1,\dots,a_{11}$ appear in this fixed order), $a_9$ wants to come after $x$, and $y$ wants to come after $a_5$. Number the gaps of the line $a_1\dots a_{11}$ as $g_0$ (before $a_1$), $g_i$ (between $a_i$ and $a_{i+1}$), $g_{11}$ (after $a_{11}$). Singer $x$ must be in one of the $9$ gaps $g_0,\dots,g_8$ and $y$ in one of the $7$ gaps $g_5,\dots,g_{11}$, independently: $9\cdot 7=63$ choices. The positions determine the order, except when $x$ and $y$ are in the same gap ($g_5,g_6,g_7,g_8$), where both orders of $x,y$ inside the gap are allowed. Total: $63+4=67$.

By the lemma, $5\cdot 6\cdot 67=2010$ is $20$-realizable.

**Answer: Yes.**

imo-isl-2010-c2.title: Example, base case N = 4, induction on N
imo-isl-2010-c2.body:
"Diagonal" means the main diagonal; in an arrangement the flag in row $i$ contributes its $i$-th field to the diagonal. Note that permuting the field positions of all flags simultaneously, swapping the two colours, or mirroring all flags (and reversing the row order) does not change the problem. Let $M_N$ be the answer.

**$M_N>2^{N-2}$.** Take the $2^{N-2}$ flags whose first field is yellow and second field is blue. In any arrangement the flag in row $1$ puts yellow and the flag in row $2$ puts blue on the diagonal, so no $N$ of them are diverse.

**$M_N\le 2^{N-2}+1$, base case $N=4$.** Take $5$ flags and split each into a left part $L$ and right part $R$, each a $2\times1$ flag from $\mathcal S=\{BB,BY,YB,YY\}$. Two $2\times1$ flags $A,C$ placed one above the other give a $2\times2$ square with monochrome diagonal iff $A_1=C_2$ or $C_1=A_2$ (choosing which one is on top). Two facts are checked directly:

1. For each $A\in\mathcal S$ there is exactly one $C\in\mathcal S$ (possibly $C=A$) such that $A,C$ do **not** form a $2\times 2$ square with monochrome diagonal: we need $C_2\ne A_1$ and $C_1\ne A_2$, which determines $C$ (for $BB$ it is $YY$, for $BY$ it is $BY$).
2. Among any three distinct elements of $\mathcal S$, two form a square with yellow diagonal and two form a square with blue diagonal. (For yellow one needs one part starting with $Y$ and another ending with $Y$: the pairs $(YB,BY),(YB,YY),(YY,BY)$; every 3-element subset of $\mathcal S$ contains one of them. Blue is symmetric.)

Let $\ell,r$ be the numbers of distinct left and right parts among the five flags. Since the flags are distinct, $5\le \ell r$, so one of them, say $r$ (by the mirror symmetry), is at least $3$; and $\ell,r\le 4$. As $r\le4<5$, two flags share a right part: $L_1R_1$ and $L_2R_1$ with $L_1\ne L_2$. As $r\ge3$, there are flags $L_3R_3,L_4R_4$ with $R_1,R_3,R_4$ distinct. Let $L'R'$ be the fifth flag. By fact 1, $L'$ forms a monochrome-diagonal $2\times2$ square with $L_1$ or with $L_2$; say with $L_2$ and say the colour is blue. By fact 2, two of the distinct right parts $R_1,R_3,R_4$ (of the flags $L_1R_1,L_3R_3,L_4R_4$) form a square with blue diagonal. Put $L'R'$ and $L_2R_1$ in rows $1,2$ (in the right order) and those two flags in rows $3,4$: the diagonal is all blue.

**Induction step.** Let $N>4$ and assume $M_{N-1}\le 2^{N-3}+1$. Take $2^{N-2}+1$ distinct flags. Some field position is not monochrome over these flags (they are distinct); assume it is the first. By pigeonhole, at least $\lceil (2^{N-2}+1)/2\rceil=2^{N-3}+1$ flags have the same first colour, say blue; call them *good*. Removing the first field of the good flags gives at least $2^{N-3}+1$ **distinct** flags of length $N-1$, so $N-1$ of them form an $(N-1)\times(N-1)$ square $Q$ with monochrome diagonal. Restore the first fields, getting $N-1$ rows of an $N\times N$ square (rows $2,\dots,N$), whose diagonal entries in positions $2,\dots,N$ are the diagonal of $Q$. It remains to choose the flag for row $1$:
- if $Q$'s diagonal is yellow, use a flag with yellow first field (it exists, and is not good, so it is unused);
- if it is blue, use an unused good flag: there are at least $2^{N-3}+1-(N-1)>0$ of them since $2^{N-3}\ge N-1$ for $N\ge5$.

Either way we get a diverse set, so $M_N\le 2^{N-2}+1$.

**Answer: $M=2^{N-2}+1$.** ∎

imo-isl-2010-c3.title: Divide the board into 2×2 blocks
imo-isl-2010-c3.body:
**Blocks.** Split the board into $50\times50$ blocks of size $2\times2$; block $(i,j)$ is in block-row $i$, block-column $j$, with $(1,1)$ top-left. A block holds at most one king (any two squares of a $2\times2$ block touch), and there are $2500$ kings in $2500$ blocks, so **every block holds exactly one king**. Label a block T or B if its king is in the top or bottom half, and L or R if it is in the left or right half (so each block is TL, TR, BL or BR). The labels determine the arrangement.

**Properties.**
- (a) If $(i,j)$ is B then $(i+1,j)$ is B (otherwise the two kings lie in adjacent rows within two adjacent columns and touch). Likewise T propagates upwards, L to the left and R to the right.
- (b) A block-column is two board columns with $25$ kings each, so it has exactly $25$ L- and $25$ R-blocks; similarly each block-row has $25$ T- and $25$ B-blocks.
- (c) Diagonal neighbours: $(i,j)$ BR and $(i+1,j+1)$ TL is impossible; $(i,j+1)$ BL and $(i+1,j)$ TR is impossible (the kings would share a vertex).

**Columns and rows are uniform.** If $(1,j)$ is B, then by (a) the whole block-column $j$ is B; call it a B-column. Block-row $1$ has $25$ B-blocks, giving $25$ B-columns with $1250$ B-blocks — all B-blocks of the board (each block-row has $25$). So the other $25$ block-columns are entirely T (*T-columns*). In the same way every block-row is entirely L or entirely R, with $25$ of each.

**Case 1: some T-column $j$ is followed by a B-column $j+1$.** Let row $i<50$ be an L-row. Then $(i,j+1)$ is BL, so by (c) $(i+1,j)$ is not TR; it is T, hence TL, and row $i+1$ is an L-row. So all rows below an L-row are L-rows: rows $1$–$25$ are R-rows and rows $26$–$50$ are L-rows. Now for any $j'$, block $(25,j')$ is R and $(26,j'+1)$ is L; by (c) we cannot have $(25,j')$ B and $(26,j'+1)$ T, i.e. a B-column is never followed by a T-column. Hence columns $1$–$25$ are T-columns and $26$–$50$ are B-columns. The arrangement is completely determined.

**Case 2: some B-column $j$ is followed by a T-column $j+1$.** Symmetrically (mirror the board left–right), the rows $1$–$25$ are L-rows, $26$–$50$ R-rows, columns $1$–$25$ B, $26$–$50$ T — again one arrangement.

Since both T- and B-columns exist, some neighbouring pair is of one of these two types, so there are at most $2$ arrangements.

**Both work.** In Case 1's arrangement, kings in vertically or horizontally neighbouring blocks have the same half-label in that direction, so they are two apart; diagonal neighbours $(i,j),(i+1,j+1)$ would need column $j$ B and column $j+1$ T (never), and $(i,j+1),(i+1,j)$ would need row $i$ L and row $i+1$ R (never). Each board row meets $25$ T-blocks (or $25$ B-blocks) and each board column $25$ L- (or R-) blocks, so it contains $25$ kings. The second arrangement is the mirror image.

**Answer: 2**

imo-isl-2010-c5.title: Count local champions and local losers
imo-isl-2010-c5.body:
Call a set of $k$ players a *$k$-company*. In a company, a *local champion* beat all other members and a *local loser* lost to all other members; each company has at most one of each.

**Counting.** Player $i$ is the local champion of exactly $\binom{w_i}{k-1}$ $k$-companies (choose the other members among the $w_i$ players he beat). So the total number of local champions of $k$-companies is $\sum_i\binom{w_i}{k-1}$, and of local losers $\sum_i\binom{\ell_i}{k-1}$.

- $k=2$: every pair has one of each, so $\sum w_i=\sum \ell_i$, i.e. $\sum(w_i-\ell_i)=0$. $\quad(4)$
- $k=3$: a 3-company is either a cycle (no champion, no loser) or transitive (one of each). Hence $\sum\left(\binom{w_i}2-\binom{\ell_i}2\right)=0$. $\quad(5)$
- $k=4$: if a 4-company has a local loser, the other three are not a cycle (that would be a bad company), so one of them beat the other two and also the loser — a local champion. So in each 4-company #losers $\le$ #champions, and $\sum\left(\binom{w_i}3-\binom{\ell_i}3\right)\ge0$. $\quad(6)$

**Identity.** For all $x,y$,
$$(x-y)^3=24\left(\binom x3-\binom y3\right)+24\left(\binom x2-\binom y2\right)-\bigl(3(x+y)^2-4\bigr)(x-y).$$
Indeed $24\binom x3+24\binom x2=4x(x-1)(x-2)+12x(x-1)=4x^3-4x$, so the right side is $4(x^3-y^3)-3(x+y)^2(x-y)=(x-y)\bigl[4(x^2+xy+y^2)-3(x+y)^2\bigr]=(x-y)^3$.

**Conclusion.** Each player played $n-1$ games, so $w_i+\ell_i=n-1$ and the coefficient $3(w_i+\ell_i)^2-4=3(n-1)^2-4$ is the same for all $i$. Summing the identity with $x=w_i$, $y=\ell_i$:
$$\sum_{i=1}^n(w_i-\ell_i)^3=24\underbrace{\sum\left(\tbinom{w_i}3-\tbinom{\ell_i}3\right)}_{\ge0}+24\underbrace{\sum\left(\tbinom{w_i}2-\tbinom{\ell_i}2\right)}_{=0}-\bigl(3(n-1)^2-4\bigr)\underbrace{\sum(w_i-\ell_i)}_{=0}\ge0. \qquad ∎$$

imo-isl-2010-c6.title: Compare three moments of the process
imo-isl-2010-c6.body:
Imagine the process continued until every string is a single pearl; let $A_i$ be the situation after step $i$ ($A_0$ the initial one). An $m$-string is a string of $m$ pearls; it is an $m$-w-string or $m$-b-string if white or black. Define

- $s$: the first index such that $A_s$ contains a 1-string (of either colour);
- $t$: the first index such that $A_t$ contains more than $k$ strings ($t=\infty$ if never);
- $f$: the first index such that all black pearls in $A_f$ are isolated.

It suffices to show that some $A_i$ with $i\le f-1$ contains a 1-w-string: then the process stops at a stage before all black pearls are isolated.

Clearly $1\le s\le f$. In step $f$ every b-string of $A_{f-1}$ becomes single pearls, so all b-strings of $A_{f-1}$ have length $1$ or $2$.

If $i\le t-1$, then $A_i$ has at most $k$ strings, so all strings longer than $1$ are cut in step $i+1$; if also $i<s$, there are no 1-strings, so **every** string is cut.

Let $B_i,b_i$ be the longest and shortest b-string lengths in $A_i$, and $W_i,w_i$ the same for w-strings.

**Claim.** For $i\le\min(s,t)$: $A_i$ has exactly $2^i$ black and $2^i$ white strings, $B_i\ge W_i$ and $b_i\ge w_i$.
*Proof.* Induction; $i=0$ is clear as $b>w$. For $1\le i\le\min(s,t)$, step $i$ starts from $A_{i-1}$ with $i-1<s$ and $i-1<t$, so every string is cut; the numbers double, and $B_i=\lceil B_{i-1}/2\rceil\ge\lceil W_{i-1}/2\rceil=W_i$, $b_i=\lfloor b_{i-1}/2\rfloor\ge\lfloor w_{i-1}/2\rfloor=w_i$. $\square$

**Case 1: $s\le t$ or $f\le t+1$.** In both situations $s\le t+1$ (as $s\le f$), so the Claim applies to $A_{s-1}$, where moreover no 1-strings exist: $B_{s-1}\ge W_{s-1}\ge w_{s-1}>1$ and $B_{s-1}\ge b_{s-1}\ge w_{s-1}$.

If $s=f$, then the b-strings of $A_{s-1}=A_{f-1}$ have length $\le2$, hence exactly $2$, so $2=B_{s-1}\ge W_{s-1}\ge w_{s-1}\ge2$: all strings of $A_{s-1}$ have length $2$, with $2^{s-1}$ of each colour, giving $b=2^s=w$ — contradicting $b>w$. So $s\le f-1$, and therefore $s\le t$ in both sub-situations. Thus in step $s$ every string of $A_{s-1}$ is cut, and a 1-string appears in $A_s$. If it is white we are done ($s<f$). If it is black, some b-string of $A_{s-1}$ has length $2$ or $3$, so $b_{s-1}\le3$, hence $2\le w_{s-1}\le b_{s-1}\le 3$, and cutting the shortest w-string (length $2$ or $3$) also produces a 1-w-string in $A_s$, with $s\le f-1$.

**Case 2: $t+1\le s$ and $t+2\le f$.** By the Claim, $A_t$ has $2^t$ white and $2^t$ black strings, all longer than $1$ (as $t<s$), and $2^{t+1}>k\ge 2^t$ (the first inequality by the definition of $t$; the second because $A_{t-1}$ has $2^t$ strings when $t\ge1$, and trivially when $t=0$). In step $t+1$ exactly $k$ strings are cut, at most $2^t$ of them black, so at least $k-2^t$ white strings are cut and $A_{t+1}$ has at least $2^t+(k-2^t)=k$ white strings. The number of white strings never decreases, so $A_{f-1}$ (note $f-1\ge t+1$) has at least $k$ white strings.

In step $f$ at least one 2-b-string is cut (the last non-isolated black pearls), so at most $k-1$ white strings are cut, and some white string $\mathcal W$ of $A_{f-1}$ is not cut. But since a 2-b-string was chosen, every string longer than $2$ and every white string of length $2$ precedes it in the ordering and was chosen too. Hence $\mathcal W$ has length $1$: an isolated white pearl exists in $A_{f-1}$.

In both cases the first isolated white pearl appears while some black string still has at least two pearls. ∎

imo-isl-2010-c7.title: Translate to a grid covering and use Hall's lemma
imo-isl-2010-c7.body:
Progressions are two-sided with positive steps $d_1,\dots,d_s$. If $n=1$ the claim is $s\ge1$. Let $n>1$; then no $d_j$ equals $1$ (otherwise $P_j=\mathbb Z$ and condition (ii) forces $s=1$, $n=1$).

**Grids.** For positive integers $n_1,\dots,n_K$ (all $\ge2$), the *grid* is $N=\{(a_1,\dots,a_K):0\le a_i\le n_i-1\}$. A *subgrid* is a set obtained by fixing the coordinates in a nonempty index set $I$:
$L=\{b\in N:\ b_i=x_i\ \ (i\in I)\}$; it is *orthogonal* to axis $i$ if $i\in I$.

**Lemma.** If $N$ is covered by subgrids $L_1,\dots,L_s$ such that (ii') each $L_m$ contains a point not covered by the others and (iii) for every axis some $L_m$ is orthogonal to it, then $s\ge1+\sum_{i=1}^K(n_i-1)$.

*Proof.* Suppose $s\le s':=\sum(n_i-1)$. Build a bipartite graph with left side $V=\{L_1,\dots,L_s\}$ and right side $V'=\{v_{ij}:1\le i\le K,\ 1\le j\le n_i-1\}$ ($|V'|=s'$), joining $L_m$ to $v_{ij}$ iff $L_m$ is orthogonal to axis $i$. For $X\subseteq V$ let $f(X)$ be its set of neighbours. By (iii), $f(V)=V'$.

Let $W\subseteq V$ be a set of maximal size with $|W|>|f(W)|$ ($W=\varnothing$ if none). Put $W'=f(W)$, $U=V\setminus W$, $U'=V'\setminus W'$. Since $|f(V)|=|V'|\ge |V|$, $W\ne V$, so $U\ne\varnothing$. The vertices $v_{i1},\dots,v_{i,n_i-1}$ have the same neighbours, so $W'$ consists of whole groups; renumber the axes so that $U'=\{v_{ij}:i\le\ell\}$ and $W'=\{v_{ij}:i>\ell\}$.

*Hall's condition in $U\cup U'$.* For $X\subseteq U$ we claim $|f(X)\cap U'|\ge|X|$. Otherwise, for nonempty $X$, using $|W|\ge|f(W)|$,
$$|W\cup X|=|W|+|X|>|f(W)|+|f(X)\cap U'|=|f(W)\cup(f(X)\cap U')|=|f(W\cup X)|,$$
contradicting the maximality of $W$. So by Hall's lemma we can assign to each $L\in U$ a distinct $v_{ij}\in U'$ adjacent to it; write $g(L)=i\le\ell$. For each $i\le\ell$ at most $n_i-1$ subgrids $L\in U$ have $g(L)=i$, and each of them is orthogonal to axis $i$, so all its points have the same $i$-th coordinate $c_L$.

*An uncovered point.* Pick $L_0\in U$; by (ii') it has a point $b$ not covered by any other subgrid, in particular by none in $W$. For each $i\le\ell$ choose $a_i\in\{0,\dots,n_i-1\}$ different from the at most $n_i-1$ values $c_L$ with $g(L)=i$, and set $a=(a_1,\dots,a_\ell,b_{\ell+1},\dots,b_K)$.
- $a\notin L$ for $L\in U$: its $g(L)$-th coordinate is $a_{g(L)}\ne c_L$.
- $a\notin L$ for $L\in W$: otherwise, since $b\notin L$ and $a,b$ differ only in the first $\ell$ coordinates, $L$ must fix some coordinate $i\le\ell$; then $L$ is adjacent to $v_{i1}\in U'$, so $v_{i1}\in f(W)=W'$, a contradiction.

So $a$ is uncovered, contradicting the covering. $\square$

**Translation.** For each $i$ some step $d_{j(i)}$ is divisible by $p_i^{\alpha_i}$. For an integer $m$, let $m_i$ be its residue mod $p_i^{\alpha_i}$, with base-$p_i$ digits $r_{i1}$ (least significant), $r_{i2},\dots,r_{i\alpha_i}$, and put
$$r(m)=(r_{11},\dots,r_{1\alpha_1},\ r_{21},\dots,\ r_{k\alpha_k})$$
— a point of the grid with $\alpha_i$ axes of size $p_i$ for each $i$. By the Chinese remainder theorem $r(m)=r(m')\iff n\mid m-m'$, so $r$ is a bijection from residues mod $n$ onto $N$ (both have $n$ elements).

Let $L_j=r(P_j)$ and $d_j=\prod p_i^{\gamma_i}$ (so $\gamma_i\le\alpha_i$, not all $0$). For $q\in P_j$ and any $q'$:
$$q'\in P_j\iff p_i^{\gamma_i}\mid q-q'\ \ \forall i\iff r_{it}(q')=r_{it}(q)\ \text{ for all } i \text{ and } t\le\gamma_i .$$
So $L_j$ is the subgrid obtained by fixing the coordinates $(i,t)$, $t\le\gamma_i$. Now:
- the $L_j$ cover $N$, since every integer lies in some $P_j$;
- (iii): $L_{j(i)}$ fixes all coordinates $(i,1),\dots,(i,\alpha_i)$;
- (ii'): if $m\in P_j$ lies in no other progression and $r(m)\in L_{j'}$ with $j'\ne j$, then $r(m)=r(m')$ for some $m'\in P_{j'}$, so $n\mid m-m'$, hence $d_{j'}\mid m-m'$ and $m\in P_{j'}$ — impossible.

The Lemma, with $\alpha_i$ axes of size $p_i$ for each $i$, gives
$$s\ge1+\sum_{i=1}^k\alpha_i(p_i-1). \qquad ∎$$

imo-isl-2010-g1.title: Angle chasing with two cyclic quadrilaterals
imo-isl-2010-g1.body:
Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ be the angles of $ABC$. Because of the right angles at $D,E,F$, the quadrilaterals $BCEF$ and $CAFD$ are cyclic, hence
$$\angle AFE=\angle BCE=\gamma,\qquad \angle DFB=\angle DCA=\gamma,\qquad \angle BDF=180^\circ-\angle FDC=\angle CAF=\alpha .$$
The line $EF$ meets the circumcircle twice; there are two cases.

**Case 1: $P$ lies on ray $EF$ beyond $F$** (on arc $AB$). Then $\angle PBA<\angle BCA=\gamma$, so
$$\angle PBD+\angle BDF=\angle PBA+\beta+\alpha<\gamma+\beta+\alpha=180^\circ,$$
and the lines $BP$, $DF$ meet at $Q$ on the extensions of $BP$ beyond $P$ and of $DF$ beyond $F$. From the cyclic quadrilateral $APBC$,
$$\angle QPA=180^\circ-\angle APB=\angle BCA=\gamma,$$
and $\angle QFA=\angle DFB=\gamma$ (vertical angles). So $\angle QPA=\angle QFA$ and $AQPF$ is cyclic. Then
$$\angle AQP=180^\circ-\angle PFA=\angle AFE=\gamma .$$

**Case 2: $P$ lies on ray $FE$ beyond $E$** (on arc $AC$). Now $Q$ lies inside segment $FD$, and
$$\angle QPA=\angle BPA=\angle BCA=\gamma=\angle DFB=180^\circ-\angle AFQ,$$
so $AFQP$ is cyclic, and $\angle AQP=\angle AFP=\angle AFE=\gamma$.

In both cases $\angle AQP=\angle QPA=\gamma$, so triangle $AQP$ is isosceles with $AP=AQ$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-g3.title: A corner circumcircle contains P
imo-isl-2010-g3.body:
Indices are taken mod $n$ ($A_{n+1}=A_1$, etc.). Note that $X_i$ and $P_i$ lie on side $A_iA_{i+1}$. By continuity it suffices to treat the case when every $X_i$ lies in the interior of its side (the inequality is preserved under limits).

**Lemma.** If $Q$ lies inside the polygon, then $Q$ lies inside or on the circumcircle of one of the triangles $X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$.

*Proof.* The polygon is the union of the convex polygon $X_1X_2\dots X_n$ and the corner triangles $X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$. If $Q$ is in a corner triangle we are done. Otherwise $Q$ is inside $X_1\dots X_n$, so $\sum_i\angle X_iQX_{i+1}=2\pi$, while $\sum_i\angle X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$ is the angle sum of the polygon, $(n-2)\pi$. Hence
$$\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(\angle X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}+\angle X_iQX_{i+1}\bigr)=n\pi,$$
so for some $i$, $\angle X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}+\angle X_iQX_{i+1}\ge\pi$. In the convex quadrilateral $QX_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$ ($Q$ and $A_{i+1}$ on opposite sides of $X_iX_{i+1}$) this means exactly that $Q$ is inside or on the circumcircle of $X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$. $\square$

**Main argument.** Apply the lemma to $Q=P$: for some $i$, $P$ lies in the closed disc bounded by the circumcircle $\Omega$ (radius $R$) of $X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$. Since $\angle PP_iA_{i+1}=\angle PP_{i+1}A_{i+1}=90^\circ$, the points $P_i,P_{i+1}$ lie on the circle $\omega$ with diameter $A_{i+1}P$; its radius is $r=\tfrac12A_{i+1}P$. As $A_{i+1}$ and $P$ are both in the closed disc of $\Omega$, $A_{i+1}P\le 2R$, i.e. $r\le R$.

Both $\angle P_iA_{i+1}P_{i+1}$ and $\angle X_iA_{i+1}X_{i+1}$ equal the polygon's angle $\varphi$ at $A_{i+1}$. By the extended law of sines in $\omega$ and in $\Omega$,
$$P_iP_{i+1}=2r\sin\varphi\le 2R\sin\varphi=X_iX_{i+1}.$$
Hence $\dfrac{X_iX_{i+1}}{P_iP_{i+1}}\ge1$, and the maximum is at least $1$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-g5.title: Complete a parallelogram and reflect D
imo-isl-2010-g5.body:
Let $T$ be the point on ray $AE$ with $AT=AB$. Since $AE\parallel BC$, $\angle CBT=\angle ATB=\angle ABT$, so $BT$ bisects $\angle ABC$ and
$$\angle ATB=\tfrac12\angle ABC .$$
Also $AE<AB=AT$, so $E$ lies between $A$ and $T$ and $ET=AT-AE=AB-AE=BC$. The segments $BC$ and $ET$ are parallel, equal and equally directed, so $BCTE$ is a parallelogram; hence the midpoint $M$ of its diagonal $CE$ is also the midpoint of $BT$. The point reflection in $M$ swaps $B\leftrightarrow T$ and $C\leftrightarrow E$.

Let $K$ be the reflection of $D$ in $M$. Since $OM\perp DM$, the line $OM$ is the perpendicular bisector of $DK$, so $OK=OD$ and $K$ lies on the circumcircle of $BCD$. Hence $\angle BKC=\angle BDC$. The reflection in $M$ maps angle $BKC$ to angle $TDE$, so
$$\angle TDE=\angle BKC=\angle BDC .$$
Therefore
$$\angle BDT=\angle BDE+\angle EDT=\angle BDE+\angle BDC=\angle CDE=\angle ABC=180^\circ-\angle BAT ,$$
using $AT\parallel BC$ in the last step. Since $A$ and $D$ lie on opposite sides of $BT$, the quadrilateral $ABDT$ is cyclic, and
$$\angle ADB=\angle ATB=\tfrac12\angle ABC=\tfrac12\angle CDE .$$
That is, $2\angle BDA=\angle CDE$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-g6.title: The incenter of ABC is inside the incircle of XYZ
imo-isl-2010-g6.body:
Let $I$, $r$ be the incenter and inradius of $ABC$, and $O$, $r'$ the incenter and inradius of the equilateral triangle $XYZ$; its circumradius is $R'=2r'$. We prove $OI<r'$ (or $O=I$), so $I$ lies inside the incircle of $XYZ$, hence inside $XYZ$.

Let the incircle of $ABC$ touch $BC,CA,AB$ at $A_1,B_1,C_1$. The three lines $IA_1,IB_1,IC_1$ divide the plane into six angles. Each is bounded by one of the rays $IA_1,IB_1,IC_1$ and the extension beyond $I$ of another; e.g. the angle between ray $IC_1$ and the extension of $A_1I$ beyond $I$ equals $180^\circ-\angle A_1IC_1=\angle B<90^\circ$. So all six angles are acute. Assume $O\ne I$ and, by symmetry, that $O$ lies in the angle bounded by ray $IC_1$ and the extension of $A_1I$ beyond $I$; this angle equals $\angle B$.

Let $A'$ and $C'$ be the projections of $O$ onto lines $IA_1$ and $IC_1$. As the angle is acute, $A'$ lies on the extension of $A_1I$ beyond $I$ and $C'$ lies on ray $IC_1$.

- **$IA'\le R'-r$.** $X$ is on $BC$ and $OX=R'$, so $d(O,BC)\le R'$. Since $OA'\parallel BC$ (both perpendicular to $IA_1$), $d(O,BC)=d(A',BC)=A'I+r$. Hence $IA'\le R'-r$.
- **$IC'\le r-r'$.** The incircle of $XYZ$ lies inside $ABC$, so $d(O,AB)\ge r'$. As $O$ is inside $ABC$, $d(O,AB)=C'C_1=r-IC'$. Hence $IC'\le r-r'$.
- **$A'O<IC'$.** Let $\theta_1=\angle OIA'$ and $\theta_2=\angle OIC'$. Then $\theta_1+\theta_2=\angle B<90^\circ$, so $\theta_2<90^\circ-\theta_1$. In the right triangles $OA'I$ and $OC'I$, $A'O=OI\sin\theta_1=OI\cos(90^\circ-\theta_1)<OI\cos\theta_2=IC'$.

Therefore
$$OI\le IA'+A'O<IA'+IC'\le(R'-r)+(r-r')=R'-r'=r'.$$
So $I$ lies strictly inside the incircle of $XYZ$, hence inside triangle $XYZ$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-g7.title: Radius is proportional to the distance from AC
imo-isl-2010-g7.body:
Let $O_i,R_i$ be the centre and radius of $\gamma_i$, let $H$ be the half-plane (bounded by $AC$) containing the figure, and for $P\in H$ let $d(P)$ be its distance to line $AC$. Write $\Omega(P,r)$ for the circle with centre $P$ and radius $r$.

**Lemma 1.** For $i<j$, the circles $\Omega(P,r)$ in $H$ tangent to $h_i$ and $h_j$ have centres on the bisector $\beta_{ij}$ of the angle between $h_i,h_j$, and $r=u_{ij}\,d(P)$ for a constant $u_{ij}$.
*Proof.* The centre is equidistant from the two rays, hence on $\beta_{ij}$. Any two such circles are homothetic with centre $B$; since $B\in AC$, the homothety multiplies $r$ and $d(P)$ by the same factor. Conversely, every circle with centre $P\in\beta_{ij}$ and $r=u_{ij}d(P)$ touches both rays. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** For $i<j$, the circles $\Omega(P,r)$ in $H$ tangent externally to $\gamma_i$ and internally to $\gamma_j$ have centres on an elliptic arc $\varepsilon_{ij}$ from $A$ to $C$, and $r=v_{ij}\,d(P)$ for a constant $v_{ij}$.
*Proof.* (a) The tangency conditions are $O_iP=R_i+r$ and $O_jP=R_j-r$, so $O_iP+O_jP=R_i+R_j=O_iA+O_jA=O_iC+O_jC$: $P$ lies on the ellipse with foci $O_i,O_j$ through $A$ and $C$; let $\varepsilon_{ij}$ be its arc $AC$ inside $H$. Conversely, this arc lies between $\gamma_i$ and $\gamma_j$, so for $P\in\varepsilon_{ij}$ we have $O_iP>R_i$, $O_jP<R_j$, and $r=O_iP-R_i=R_j-O_jP>0$ gives a circle with both tangencies.

(b) Put vectors from $A$: $\vec\rho=\vec{AP}$, $\vec\rho_i=\vec{AO_i}$, $\vec\rho_j=\vec{AO_j}$, with $|\vec\rho_i|=R_i$, $|\vec\rho_j|=R_j$. Both $O_i,O_j$ lie on the perpendicular bisector of $AC$, so $\vec\rho_j-\vec\rho_i=d_{ij}\vec v$, where $\vec v$ is the unit normal to $AC$ pointing into $H$ and $d_{ij}$ is a constant; also $\vec\rho\cdot\vec v=d(P)$. Subtracting $|\vec\rho-\vec\rho_j|^2=(R_j-r)^2$ from $|\vec\rho-\vec\rho_i|^2=(R_i+r)^2$:
$$R_i^2-R_j^2+2\vec\rho\cdot(\vec\rho_j-\vec\rho_i)=R_i^2-R_j^2+2r(R_i+R_j)\ \Longrightarrow\ d_{ij}\,d(P)=r(R_i+R_j).$$
So $r=v_{ij}d(P)$ with $v_{ij}=\dfrac{d_{ij}}{R_i+R_j}$, independent of $P$. $\square$

**Lemma 3.** The curved quadrilateral bounded by $h_i,h_{i+1}$ and $\gamma_j,\gamma_{j+1}$ is circumscribed if and only if $u_{i,i+1}=v_{j,j+1}$.
*Proof.* If its inscribed circle is $\Omega(P,r)$, Lemmas 1 and 2 give $r=u_{i,i+1}d(P)=v_{j,j+1}d(P)$, and $d(P)>0$. Conversely, if $u_{i,i+1}=v_{j,j+1}$, let $P$ be the intersection of the ray $\beta_{i,i+1}$ (starting at $B\in AC$) with the arc $\varepsilon_{j,j+1}$ (which together with segment $AC$ bounds a region containing $B$ on its boundary), and take $r=u_{i,i+1}d(P)=v_{j,j+1}d(P)$. By Lemma 1 the circle touches $h_i,h_{i+1}$, and by Lemma 2 it touches $\gamma_j,\gamma_{j+1}$. $\square$

**Conclusion.** The three given circumscribed quadrilaterals are those bounded by $(h_1,h_2;\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$, $(h_1,h_2;\gamma_2,\gamma_3)$ and $(h_2,h_3;\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$, so by Lemma 3
$$u_{12}=v_{12},\qquad u_{12}=v_{23},\qquad u_{23}=v_{12}.$$
Hence $u_{23}=v_{12}=u_{12}=v_{23}$, and by Lemma 3 the quadrilateral bounded by $(h_2,h_3;\gamma_2,\gamma_3)$, i.e. $\widehat{V_{22}V_{32}}\widehat{V_{33}V_{23}}$, is circumscribed. ∎

imo-isl-2010-n1.title: Compare with a telescoping product
imo-isl-2010-n1.body:
**Lower bound.** Order the numbers $s_1<s_2<\dots<s_n$. No $s_i$ equals $1$ (that factor would be $0$), so $2\le s_1$ and, being distinct integers, $s_i\ge i+1$. Hence
$$\frac{51}{2010}=\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-\frac1{s_i}\right)\ge\prod_{i=1}^n\left(1-\frac1{i+1}\right)=\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdots\frac{n}{n+1}=\frac1{n+1},$$
so $n+1\ge\frac{2010}{51}=\frac{670}{17}>39$, i.e. $n\ge 39$.

**Example with $n=39$.** Take $\{2,3,\dots,33\}\cup\{35,36,\dots,40\}\cup\{67\}$ ($32+6+1=39$ numbers). Each factor is $\frac{s-1}{s}$, and the products telescope:
$$\frac12\cdot\frac23\cdots\frac{32}{33}\cdot\frac{34}{35}\cdots\frac{39}{40}\cdot\frac{66}{67}=\frac1{33}\cdot\frac{34}{40}\cdot\frac{66}{67}=\frac{17}{670}=\frac{51}{2010}.$$

**Answer: 39**

imo-isl-2010-n2.title: Small n by hand, then 3-adic bounds
imo-isl-2010-n2.body:
**Small $n$.** For fixed $n$ the equation is a quadratic in $m$:

| $n$ | equation | discriminant | integer roots |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | $m^2-m+2=0$ | $-7$ | none |
| 1 | $m^2-3m+6=0$ | $-15$ | none |
| 2 | $m^2-7m+18=0$ | $-23$ | none |
| 3 | $m^2-15m+54=0$ | $9$ | $6,\ 9$ |
| 4 | $m^2-31m+162=0$ | $313$ | none |
| 5 | $m^2-63m+486=0$ | $2025=45^2$ | $9,\ 54$ |

**No solutions for $n\ge6$.** Let $(m,n)$ be a solution with $n\ge 6$. Clearly $m>0$ and $m\mid m(2^{n+1}-1)-m^2=2\cdot3^n$, so $m=3^p$ or $m=2\cdot3^q$ with $0\le p,q\le n$. Then $2^{n+1}-1=m+\frac{2\cdot3^n}{m}$ equals $3^p+2\cdot3^{n-p}$ or $2\cdot3^q+3^{n-q}$. In both cases there are $p,q\ge0$ with
$$3^p+2\cdot3^q=2^{n+1}-1,\qquad p+q=n. \qquad(2)$$

*Bounds.* From (2), $3^p<2^{n+1}=8^{\frac{n+1}3}<9^{\frac{n+1}3}=3^{\frac{2(n+1)}3}$ and $2\cdot3^q<2^{n+1}=2\cdot8^{\frac n3}<2\cdot3^{\frac{2n}3}$. So $p,q<\frac{2(n+1)}3$, and with $p+q=n$,
$$\frac{n-2}{3}<p,q<\frac{2(n+1)}3. \qquad(3)$$

*Divisibility.* Let $h=\min(p,q)$; by (3), $h>\frac{n-2}3\ge\frac43$, so $h\ge2$. Both terms on the left of (2) are divisible by $3^h$, so $9\mid 3^h\mid 2^{n+1}-1$. The order of $2$ modulo $9$ is $6$, so $6\mid n+1$; write $n+1=6r$. Then
$$2^{n+1}-1=4^{3r}-1=(4^{2r}+4^r+1)(2^r-1)(2^r+1).$$
The first factor equals $(4^r-1)^2+3\cdot4^r$; since $3\mid4^r-1$, it is divisible by $3$ but not by $9$. The factors $2^r-1$ and $2^r+1$ are odd and differ by $2$, so they are coprime. As $3^h$ divides the product, $3^{h-1}$ divides $2^r-1$ or $2^r+1$, so
$$3^{h-1}\le 2^r+1\le 3^r=3^{\frac{n+1}6}.$$
Hence $\frac{n-2}3-1<h-1\le\frac{n+1}6$, which gives $n<11$. But $n\ge6$ and $6\mid n+1$ force $n\ge11$ — a contradiction.

**Answer:** $(6,3),\ (9,3),\ (9,5),\ (54,5)$. ∎

imo-isl-2010-n3.title: Reduce to integers and use squares mod 8 (infinite descent)
imo-isl-2010-n3.body:
**$n=5$ works:** $x^2+7=x^2+2^2+1^2+1^2+1^2$.

**Four polynomials are not enough.** Suppose $x^2+7=\sum_{i=1}^4 f_i(x)^2$ with rational coefficients (some $f_i$ may be $0$). If the largest degree $d$ of the $f_i$ were $\ge2$, the coefficient of $x^{2d}$ on the right would be a sum of squares of nonzero leading coefficients, hence positive — impossible. So $f_i(x)=a_ix+b_i$ with rationals $a_i,b_i$, and comparing coefficients,
$$\sum a_i^2=1,\qquad \sum a_ib_i=0,\qquad \sum b_i^2=7 .$$
Let $p_i=a_i+b_i$ and $q_i=a_i-b_i$. Then
$$\sum p_i^2=1+0+7=8,\qquad \sum q_i^2=8,\qquad \sum p_iq_i=\sum a_i^2-\sum b_i^2=-6 .$$
Multiplying by a common denominator $m>0$, we get integers $x_i=mp_i$, $y_i=mq_i$ with
$$\text{(i) } \sum x_i^2=8m^2,\qquad \text{(ii) } \sum y_i^2=8m^2,\qquad \text{(iii) } \sum x_iy_i=-6m^2 .$$
Take such a solution with $m>0$ minimal. A square is $\equiv1\pmod 8$ if odd and $\equiv 0$ or $4\pmod8$ if even. If $c$ of the $x_i$ are odd, then $\sum x_i^2\equiv c\pmod 4$, so $c\in\{0,4\}$; but $c=4$ gives $\sum x_i^2\equiv4\pmod 8$, not $0$. So $c=0$: all $x_i$ are even, and likewise all $y_i$. Then $4\mid\sum x_iy_i=-6m^2$, so $m$ is even. Now $(x_i/2,\ y_i/2,\ m/2)$ is a smaller solution of (i)–(iii), contradicting minimality.

Hence $n\ge5$.

**Answer: 5**

imo-isl-2010-n4.title: Work modulo 67
imo-isl-2010-n4.body:
Note $P(m)-P(k)=(m-k)\bigl(a(m^2+mk+k^2)+b\bigr)$.

**(a)** Take $P(x)=x^3-51^2x$, i.e. $(a,b)=(1,-51^2)$.
- *Not very good:* $P(51)=0=P(0)$, so for any $n\nmid 51$ we have $n\mid P(51)-P(0)$ but $n\nmid 51-0$. Only the finitely many divisors of $51$ can be good $n$.
- *51-good:* if $51\mid P(m)-P(k)$ then $m^3\equiv k^3\pmod{51}$. Modulo $3$, Fermat gives $m\equiv m^3\equiv k^3\equiv k$. Modulo $17$, since $33\equiv1\pmod{16}$, Fermat gives $m\equiv m^{33}=(m^3)^{11}\equiv(k^3)^{11}\equiv k$ (also true when $17\mid m$). So $51\mid m-k$.

**(b)** Let $(a,b)$ be 2010-good; note $2010=30\cdot67$.

*Claim 1: $(a,b)$ is 67-good.* Let $67\mid P(m)-P(k)$. By the Chinese remainder theorem choose $m'\equiv m$, $k'\equiv k\pmod{67}$ with $m'\equiv k'\equiv0\pmod{30}$. Then $P(m')\equiv P(0)\equiv P(k')\pmod{30}$ and $P(m')\equiv P(m)\equiv P(k)\equiv P(k')\pmod{67}$, so $2010\mid P(m')-P(k')$, hence $2010\mid m'-k'$ and $m\equiv m'\equiv k'\equiv k\pmod{67}$. $\square$

*Claim 2: $67\mid a$.* Suppose not. The $34$ numbers $at^2$ ($0\le t\le 33$) are distinct mod $67$ (as $t^2\equiv t'^2$ forces $t\equiv\pm t'$), and so are the $34$ numbers $-3as^2-b$ ($0\le s\le33$). As $34+34>67$, some $at^2\equiv-3as^2-b\pmod{67}$. Put $m=t\pm s$, $k=\mp2s$. Then $m-k=t\pm3s$ and $m^2+mk+k^2=t^2+3s^2$, so
$$P(m)-P(k)=(t\pm3s)\bigl(at^2+3as^2+b\bigr)\equiv0\pmod{67}$$
for both sign choices. By 67-goodness, $t+3s\equiv t-3s\equiv0$, so $t\equiv s\equiv0$ and then $b\equiv-3as^2-at^2\equiv0\pmod{67}$. But then $P(7)-P(2)=335a+5b=67\cdot5a+5b\equiv0\pmod{67}$ while $67\nmid 5$ — contradicting 67-goodness. $\square$

*Claim 3: $(a,b)$ is $67^i$-good for all $i\ge1$.* By Claim 2, $67\mid a$. If also $67\mid b$, then $P(x)\equiv0\pmod{67}$ for all $x$, contradicting 67-goodness; so $67\nmid b$. If $67^i\mid P(m)-P(k)=(m-k)\bigl(a(m^2+mk+k^2)+b\bigr)$, the second factor is $\equiv b\not\equiv0\pmod{67}$, so it is coprime to $67$ and $67^i\mid m-k$. $\square$

Thus every 2010-good pair is $67^i$-good for all $i$, hence very good. ∎

imo-isl-2010-n6.title: Count the cycles of Fibonacci-type sequences mod 2^n
imo-isl-2010-n6.body:
Denote the $j$-th cell of row $i$ by $(i,j)$; everything is mod $2^n$.

**Reduction to cycles.** Draw an arrow $(i,j)\to(j,i+j)$ from each cell. Every cell has exactly one outgoing arrow and exactly one incoming arrow (from $(k-j,j)$ into $(j,k)$), so the cells split into disjoint cycles. The condition says exactly that cells joined by an arrow have the same colour, so each cycle is monochromatic, and giving each cycle its own colour is allowed. Hence **the maximal number of colours equals the number of cycles**; we show it is $2^n$.

The cycle through $(i,j)$ is $(a_0,a_1),(a_1,a_2),\dots$ where $a_0=i$, $a_1=j$, $a_{t+1}=a_t+a_{t-1}$ (a *Fibonacci-type* sequence); its length is the period $p_n(A)$ of $A=(a_t)$ modulo $2^n$.

Let $F_0=0,F_1=1,F_{t+2}=F_{t+1}+F_t$, $F_{-1}=1$, and let $\nu(x)$ be the exponent of $2$ in $x$.

**Lemma 1.** For a Fibonacci-type sequence, $a_t=F_{t-1}a_0+F_ta_1$ for $t\ge0$. (Induction: both sides satisfy the same recursion and agree for $t=0,1$.)

**Lemma 2.** For $m\ge3$: (a) $\nu(F_{3\cdot2^{m-2}})=m$; (b) $3\cdot2^{m-2}$ is the least positive index $d$ with $2^m\mid F_d$; (c) $F_{3\cdot2^{m-2}+1}\equiv1+2^{m-1}\pmod{2^m}$.

*Proof.* Induction on $m$. For $m=3$: $F_6=8$, none of $F_1,\dots,F_5=1,1,2,3,5$ is divisible by $8$, and $F_7=13\equiv1+4\pmod8$. Let $m>3$ and $k=3\cdot2^{m-3}$. Lemma 1 applied to $F_k,F_{k+1},\dots$ gives
$$F_{2k}=F_{k-1}F_k+F_kF_{k+1}=2F_{k+1}F_k-F_k^2,\qquad F_{2k+1}=F_k^2+F_{k+1}^2 .$$
By hypothesis $\nu(F_k)=m-1$ and $F_{k+1}\equiv1+2^{m-2}\pmod{2^{m-1}}$ is odd. So $\nu(F_k^2)=2m-2>m=\nu(2F_kF_{k+1})$, giving $\nu(F_{2k})=m$: (a). Writing $F_{k+1}=1+2^{m-2}(1+2c)$,
$$F_{2k+1}\equiv F_{k+1}^2=1+2^{m-1}(1+2c)+2^{2m-4}(1+2c)^2\equiv1+2^{m-1}\pmod{2^m}$$
as $2m-4\ge m$: (c). For (b), suppose $2^m\mid F_\ell$ with $0<\ell<2k$. Then $2^{m-1}\mid F_\ell$, so $\ell\ge k$ by the hypothesis, and $\ell\ne k$ by (a) for $m-1$; so $0<\ell-k<k$. By Lemma 1, $F_\ell=F_{k-1}F_{\ell-k}+F_kF_{\ell-k+1}$. The second term is divisible by $2^{m-1}$; in the first, $F_{k-1}=F_{k+1}-F_k$ is odd and $2^{m-1}\nmid F_{\ell-k}$ by minimality of $k$. So $2^{m-1}\nmid F_\ell$, a contradiction. $\square$

**2-adic level.** For $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$ put $\mu(a,b)=\min(\nu(a),\nu(b))$. Since $\mu(a_0,a_1)=\mu(a_1,a_0+a_1)$, $\mu$ is constant along a Fibonacci-type sequence; write $\mu(A)$.

**Lemma 3.** If $\mu(A)=k<n$, then $p_n(A)=3\cdot2^{n-1-k}$.

*Proof.* $A$ has period $p$ mod $2^n$ iff $A/2^k$ has period $p$ mod $2^{n-k}$, and $\mu(A/2^k)=0$; so it suffices to show $p_n(A)=3\cdot2^{n-1}$ when $\mu(A)=0$. Induction on $n$. For $n=1$, every such sequence is $0,1,1,0,1,1,\dots$ mod $2$ (period $3$). For $n=2$, the $12$ pairs mod $4$ with an odd entry are exactly the consecutive pairs of the two $6$-cycles $0,1,1,2,3,1$ and $0,3,3,2,1,3$, so the period is $6$.

Let $n\ge3$ and $\mu(A)=0$. A period mod $2^n$ is a period mod $2^{n-1}$, so $s:=p_{n-1}(A)=3\cdot2^{n-2}$ divides $p_n(A)$. Shifting $A$ (which does not change periods), assume $a_0$ is even (one of any three consecutive terms is even); then $a_1$ is odd. Write $a_0=2b_0+F_0$, $a_1=2b_1+F_1$ and let $B=(b_t)$ be the Fibonacci-type sequence starting with $b_0,b_1$; by linearity $a_t=2b_t+F_t$ for all $t$. By the induction hypothesis (or trivially if $B\equiv0$ or $\mu(B)\ge n-1$), $p_{n-1}(B)$ divides $s$, so $(2b_t)$ has period $s$ mod $2^n$. By Lemma 2 with $m=n$ and with $m=n+1$: $F_{s+1}\equiv1+2^{n-1}$, $F_{2s}\equiv0$, $F_{2s+1}\equiv1\pmod{2^n}$. Hence, mod $2^n$,
$$a_{s+1}\equiv2b_1+1+2^{n-1}\not\equiv a_1,\qquad a_{2s}\equiv2b_0=a_0,\qquad a_{2s+1}\equiv2b_1+1=a_1 .$$
So $s$ is not a period but $2s$ is; as $s\mid p_n(A)\mid2s$, $p_n(A)=2s=3\cdot2^{n-1}$. $\square$

**Counting.** Fix $0\le k\le n-1$. The cells $(i,j)$ with $\mu(i,j)=k$ are those with both entries divisible by $2^k$ but not both by $2^{k+1}$: there are $2^{2(n-k)}-2^{2(n-k-1)}=3\cdot2^{2n-2k-2}$ of them. They form whole cycles, each of length $3\cdot2^{n-1-k}$ by Lemma 3, so they form $2^{n-k-1}$ cycles. The cell $(0,0)$ is a cycle by itself. Altogether
$$1+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}2^{n-1-k}=1+(1+2+\dots+2^{n-1})=2^n$$
cycles, so the maximal number of colours is $2^n$. ∎
